0:
The two letters to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ and the letter to ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ are usually grouped together and called the pastoral letters, because each is addressed to a trusted colleague who has been left in charge of churches. Unlike most of ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s letters, they are written not to a congregation but to a single person, and they read like a senior leader's instructions to a deputy he knows well and trusts.

⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ is one of the most familiar figures in ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s story. Acts introduces him in the town of ⟦l:lystra_742|Lystra⟧, in the hill country of what is now southern Turkey, the son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father. Paul took him on as a young companion at the start of his second great journey, and Timothy stayed with him for years. He travelled through ⟦l:macedonia_747|Macedonia⟧ and ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧, was sent back alone to strengthen the church in ⟦l:thessalonica_1158|Thessalonica⟧, carried messages to ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧, and appears as co-sender of several of Paul's letters. Paul writes of him with unusual affection, as a son.

The setting of this letter is ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧, the great city of the Roman province of ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧, on the western coast of Asia Minor, famous across the empire for its temple of Artemis. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ had spent nearly three years there, according to Acts, and the church had grown strong. When he later met the Ephesian elders for the last time at ⟦l:miletus_801|Miletus⟧, he warned them that savage wolves would come in among them, and that men from their own number would rise up and distort the truth. This letter shows that the warning has come true. Certain teachers in the church are spreading speculations, myths and endless genealogies, arguing about the law, forbidding marriage and certain foods, and treating religion as a way to make money. Two of them, ⟦p:hymenaeus_1583|Hymenaeus⟧ and ⟦p:alexander_189|Alexander⟧, are named.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has left for ⟦l:macedonia_747|Macedonia⟧ and asked ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ to stay on in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ and set things right. He hopes to come back soon, but writes in case he is delayed, so that Timothy will know how people ought to conduct themselves in the household of God. This trip to Macedonia belongs to the years after Acts closes. Paul was released from his first imprisonment in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, travelled again in the east, and was later arrested a second time and executed, in the middle of the sixties. This letter comes from those last years, while Paul was still free to travel and Timothy was carrying the weight of a large and troubled church.

The letter moves between personal encouragement and practical instruction. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ charges ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ to confront the false teachers and remembers his own past as a persecutor shown mercy. He gives direction on prayer and public worship, on the qualities required of overseers and deacons, on caring for widows, honouring elders, the conduct of slaves, and the dangers of wealth. Throughout, he returns to Timothy himself: his youth, his health, his gifts, and the need to guard his own life as well as his teaching.

The letter's world is one of households, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ pictures the church as God's household, with its own order and its own reputation to protect among outsiders. Behind it all stands the situation in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧: a church troubled by false teaching from within, and a younger man asked to stand firm in the middle of it, with his mentor far away.
1:
The letter opens with ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s formal title, an apostle by the command of God, and a greeting to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, his true child in the faith. It is a formal opening for a letter to a son, and it puts the full weight of Paul's commission behind what Timothy is being asked to do.

Then, without a long thanksgiving, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ comes straight to the point. He reminds ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ why he was left in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧: certain men are teaching things they should not, occupying themselves with myths and endless genealogies. They want to be teachers of the law, Paul says, though they do not understand what they are saying or the things they so confidently assert. The aim of his charge is love, from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith.

In the middle of the chapter ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns to his own story. He was once a blasphemer and a violent persecutor of the church, and he speaks of the mercy that met him with evident wonder, breaking into praise as he does so. Then he returns to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, recalling prophecies spoken over him, and names two men who have shipwrecked their faith: ⟦p:hymenaeus_1583|Hymenaeus⟧ and ⟦p:alexander_189|Alexander⟧.
2:
Having charged ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ to deal with the false teachers, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ begins to address the life of the church itself, starting with its prayers when it gathers. First of all, he says, prayers should be offered for everyone, including kings and those in authority. In the Roman world, where Christians were a small and often suspected minority, that instruction had practical weight. Paul grounds it in the conviction that God desires all people to be saved, and that there is one God and one mediator, Christ ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧.

From there ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns to the conduct of men and women in public worship. Men are to pray without anger or quarrelling. Women are to dress modestly, without displays of wealth, and to learn quietly. Paul then gives restrictions on women teaching, and supports them with a reference to ⟦p:adam_78|Adam⟧ and ⟦p:eve_1231|Eve⟧, in the order of their creation and in the deception in the garden.

He closes the passage with a word of hope: women will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love and holiness, with self-control.
3:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ now turns from the gathered worship of the church to its leadership. The false teaching in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ has been spread by people within the church, and so the question of who should lead is urgent.

He describes first the overseer, a word that in these letters is used alongside the title of elder for those who led and taught the congregation. The qualities he lists are mostly about character and reputation: self-control, hospitality, the ability to teach, freedom from the love of money, a well-ordered household, and a good name among outsiders. He then turns to deacons, who served the church in practical ways, with a similar emphasis on integrity, and with a brief word to the women, who are likewise to be dignified and faithful in all things.

The chapter closes by stepping back. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ hopes to visit soon, but writes in case he is delayed, so that ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ will know how to conduct himself in God's household. He ends with a short confession about Christ, set out like lines of an early hymn.
4:
The hymn that closed chapter three celebrated the truth about Christ. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ now turns sharply to its opposite. The Spirit has warned, he says, that in later times some will abandon the faith and follow deceiving spirits. He describes the result in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ with some precision: teachers who forbid marriage and insist on abstaining from certain foods.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ answers with the goodness of creation. Everything God made is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. The words echo the first chapter of Genesis, where God looks on all he has made and calls it good.

The second half of the chapter is addressed to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ himself. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ contrasts physical training, which was prized in the Greek gymnasium, with training in godliness. He tells Timothy not to let anyone look down on him because he is young. By now Timothy had served with Paul for some fifteen years, yet he was still young for a leader in that culture. Paul urges him to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, to preaching and teaching, and not to neglect the gift given to him when the elders laid their hands on him.
5:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has just spoken to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ about his own example and teaching. Now he gives guidance on how Timothy should deal with different groups in the church, beginning with a principle: treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters.

Most of the chapter concerns widows. In a world with no pensions or social safety net, a woman who lost her husband could be left destitute, and the church in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ supported a number of widows from its common funds. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ sets out who should receive that support. Families must care for their own first, and the church's help is for widows who are truly alone. There was also a recognised group of older widows, enrolled on a list, devoted to prayer and good works. Paul gives cautions about younger widows, some of whom have already turned aside to follow ⟦p:satan_2476|Satan⟧.

The chapter then turns to elders: their honour and pay, how accusations against them should be handled, and the danger of appointing anyone too quickly. In the middle of it is a personal aside about ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧'s frequent stomach ailments.
6:
The final chapter brings together several threads. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ begins with slaves, who made up a large part of the population of a city like ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧. He asks believing slaves to honour their masters so that the gospel will not be discredited, including those whose masters are fellow believers.

Then he returns, one last time, to the false teachers. He describes them as conceited, quarrelsome and fond of disputes about words, and he adds a further charge: they treat godliness as a means of financial gain. That leads him into a reflection on contentment and the dangers of desiring wealth, which contains some of the most quoted words in the letter about the love of money.

The tone rises toward the end. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns directly to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, addressing him as a man of God, and charges him before God and before Christ ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, who made the good confession before ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pontius Pilate⟧, to keep the command until the Lord appears. He breaks into a doxology, adds a brief word for the rich, and closes with a final appeal, calling Timothy by name to guard what has been entrusted to him.
